The Ni-based superalloy was manufactured via a powder metallurgy process including hot isostatic pressing and hot extrusion.
The as-received superalloy contained fabrication-induced voids, which were observed in the microstructure.
The true stress-strain curves of the superalloy exhibited characteristics of dynamic recovery and dynamic recrystallization.
The peak stress decreased by ~30% when the deformation temperature increased from 1050 to 1150°C.
The peak stress at a strain rate of 0.001 s^-1 was only ~10% of that at a strain rate of 1 s^-1.
The maximum principal stress was concentrated at the outer bulging surfaces of the samples during hot compression.
The critical failure strain increased with increasing temperature in a third-order polynomial relationship.
The failure was found to be strain-controlled and largely insensitive to the range of strain rates considered.
Varying the friction coefficient between 0.3 and 1.0 did not significantly affect the stress contours and failure behavior.
The critical failure strain was determined from the FEA simulations based on the first element failure or the evolution of void volume fraction.
The processing maps with failure domains were used to define an optimized processing window for hot deformation of the superalloy.
The study established an FEA model capable of quantitatively predicting the failure threshold of powder metallurgy Ni-based superalloys.
The researchers used the Gurson-Tvergaard-Needleman (GTN) damage model to simulate the cavity-driven intergranular fracture of the superalloy.
The deformation temperature was a more controlling factor than the strain rate in the failure behaviors of the powder metallurgy Ni-based superalloy.
The study aimed to guide the production practice of the hot deformation process for powder metallurgy Ni-based superalloys.
